## 2 Samuel 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: *“Some time later, David inquired of the LORD…”*

- **David as the model of seeking God’s will.** David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/Charismatic) notes that inquiring of the LORD was “a key to success in David’s life” and that David wanted more than God’s blessing on his plans — he wanted to be right in the middle of God’s plan. Even after a period of spiritual decline in Ziklag, David sought guidance rather than rushing to seize the throne. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Not opportunistic.** Guzik also observes that David didn’t want to appear as though he only returned because Saul was dead. He was “not overly concerned with appearances before man, he was not unconcerned with appearances either.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Through the Urim.** Keil & Delitzsch (older conservative Lutheran/Reformed) and Gill (older Baptist) both state David inquired “through the Urim” by means of Abiathar the priest. Gill adds the Targum’s phrasing, “of the Word of the Lord.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/2.htm

- **A two-part question.** Precept Austin notes that the second question (“Where shall I go up?”) called for more than a yes/no answer, suggesting David may not have used the ephod with Urim and Thummim for this inquiry — though “we cannot be dogmatic.” He quotes Josephus, who says David inquired “of the prophet, not by the sacred lots.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-2-commentary

- **Patient waiting.** Precept Austin stresses David’s patience: “David could have taken the throne by force — he had the LORD’s promise … And yet … he waits on the LORD. He inquires of the LORD.” Theodore Epp is quoted: “Hebron means ‘alliance’ or ‘communion’ in contrast to Ziklag, which refers to self-will.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-2-commentary

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** David’s inquiry was made “through the high priest Abiathar, as in 1 Samuel 23:9-10.” Hebron was chosen as “peculiarly well adapted for a capital,” given its situation in the mountains, its centrality, its sacred associations (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob buried there), and its status as a priestly city and city of refuge. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 2: *“So David went there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail…”*

- **Obedience.** Precept Austin highlights the “So” (therefore): David’s unhesitating obedience to the word of the LORD. “This is a great pattern for all God’s children to imitate!” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-2-commentary

- **Ellicott:** The two wives are those mentioned in 1 Samuel 25:42-43. Ahinoam was mother of David’s first son Amnon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 3: *“David also took the men who were with him, each with his household…”*

- **Whole community moves.** Ellicott notes that David’s whole force of 600 men, with their families, accompanied him and settled in the towns of the Hebron district. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Wiersbe (Evangelical, cited at Precept Austin):** While at Ziklag, volunteers from Benjamin, Gad, and Manasseh had come to David (1 Chron. 12:1–22), so he had not only a large army but also representation from other tribes. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-2-commentary

### v. 4: *“Then the men of Judah came to Hebron, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah…”*

- **David did not seize the throne.** Guzik: “This shows that David did not seize the throne. The elders of Judah approached him. David knew that it was better to let God lift him up through others than it was to strive to advance himself.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Three anointings.** Both Guzik and Ellicott note three distinct anointings of David: (1) by Samuel privately in Bethlehem (1 Sam. 16), a token of divine commission; (2) here by Judah at Hebron, public recognition by his own tribe; (3) later by all Israel (2 Sam. 5:3). Ellicott compares this to Saul’s anointings. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Fresh anointing.** Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis): “This also shows that there is a sense in which the first anointing wasn’t enough. We need a fresh anointing from God and an ongoing experience of the Holy Spirit … This anointing couldn’t come when David still lived among the Philistines virtually as a Philistine.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Gill (older Baptist):** The “men of Judah” were the elders/principals of each city. They knew the kingdom was promised to their tribe from Genesis 49:10. Though David had been anointed by Samuel, “he is again anointed by the people, as an inauguration into his office.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/2.htm

- **Ellicott on Jabesh-gilead connection:** The men of Judah informed David that Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul. Ellicott notes Jabesh-gilead was destroyed in the civil war against Benjamin (Judges 21:9-12) and its 400 virgins given to surviving Benjamites, creating a special bond between Saul (of Benjamin) and that city. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 5: *“David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead… ‘The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord…’”*

- **Gratitude, not opportunism.** Guzik: “David showed appropriate gratitude to the men who risked their lives to honor the memory of Saul and Jonathan.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Political wisdom as well as genuine kindness.** Keil & Delitzsch: “As this expression of thanks involved a solemn recognition of the departed king, by which David divested himself of even the appearance of a rebellion, the announcement of the anointing he had received contained an indirect summons to the Jabeshites to recognise him as their king now.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Gill:** David sent thanks “for their courage and boldness in rescuing the bodies of Saul and his sons out of the hands of the Philistines, and for their civility in the burial of them.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/2.htm

### vv. 6–7: *“Now may the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness… be strong and courageous…”*

- **“Grace and truth.”** Keil & Delitzsch connect “loving devotion and faithfulness” (ḥesed we’emet) to Exodus 34:6 — “the two sides by which the goodness of God is manifested … His forgiving grace, and … His trustworthiness, or the fulfilment of His promises.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott on “I also will show you the same favor”:** The Hebrew does not directly convey future recompense. “The thought is that David, as now the rightful king of Israel, appreciates the act, and wishes to show publicly his favour.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **A call to recognize David as king.** Keil & Delitzsch: “Be strong and courageous” is a demand “that now that Saul their lord was dead, and the Judaeans had anointed him (David) king, they would show themselves valiant … in their reverence and fidelity towards David.” It required courage because Saul’s army had fled to Gilead and opposition from Abner was expected. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Guzik:** David “knew that he needed brave men like these to secure and advance his kingdom, especially in the turmoil sure to surround his ascension to the throne.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

### vv. 8–9: *“Abner son of Ner… took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth, moved him to Mahanaim, and made him king…”*

- **Abner as power behind the throne.** Guzik: “Abner made Ishbosheth king, probably so that he could be the real power behind the throne of a weak king.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Rebellion against Jehovah.** Keil & Delitzsch: Abner’s promotion of Ish-bosheth “was not only a continuation of the hostility of Saul towards David, but also an open act of rebellion against Jehovah, who had rejected Saul and chosen David prince over Israel.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott on Ish-bosheth’s name:** His original name was “Esh-baal” (fire of Baal) in 1 Chronicles 8:33, later changed to Ish-bosheth (“man of shame”), just as Jerubbaal became Jerubbesheth — the “bosheth” (shame) element replacing “Baal.” Ellicott suggests two possible reasons: the Baal-compounds may have originally been given for “manful opposition to idolatry” and later changed because of the sequel of their histories; or in Saul’s family, the Baal-compound may have been a later name marking their opposition to God’s chosen king. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Mahanaim:** Ellicott notes it was east of the Jordan, famous from Jacob’s story (Gen. 32:2), a Levitical city, safe from the Philistines, and later David’s refuge during Absalom’s revolt. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **The territories.** The list (Gilead, Asher/Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin) represents Abner’s gradual extension of Ish-bosheth’s rule. Keil & Delitzsch note the Hebrew “Ashurites” is textually uncertain; the Septuagint reads Θασιρί, the Syriac/Vulgate suggest “Geshurites”; the Chaldee reads “tribe of Asher.” Ellicott leans toward “Asherites,” representing the whole region west of the Jordan north of Esdraelon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 10–11: *“Ish-bosheth… forty years old… reigned for two years. The house of Judah… followed David. And… David was king in Hebron… seven years and six months.”*

- **The chronological puzzle — why only two years for Ish-bosheth vs. seven and a half for David?** Keil & Delitzsch reject the theory that David reigned only two years over Judah before Ish-bosheth’s death, then five and a half over Israel (contradicted by the plain text). They argue instead that Ish-bosheth was not made king immediately after Saul’s death, but only after Abner spent about five years recovering land west of the Jordan from the Philistines. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott agrees:** The time between Saul’s death and Ish-bosheth’s coronation was “probably four or five years,” since all northern territory was under Philistine control after Gilboa. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Guzik on David’s patience:** “For two years David allowed Ishbosheth to reign over most of Israel. These two years showed remarkable patience, longsuffering, and trust in God … Ishbosheth was not the LORD’s anointed like Saul — David seemed to have every right to crush this man … Yet out of trust in the LORD and respect for Saul’s memory, David waited.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Gill:** The seven years and six months in Hebron, added to thirty-three years in Jerusalem over all Israel, makes forty years and six months, “for the roundness of the number, usually called forty years” (2 Sam. 5:4). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/2.htm

### vv. 12–13: *“Abner… and the servants of Ish-bosheth… marched out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. So Joab… along with the servants of David, marched out and met them by the pool of Gibeon.”*

- **A contest for Benjamin.** Ellicott notes Gibeon was in Benjamin’s territory, about five and a half miles northwest of Jerusalem. The generals “met, possibly by design, but more likely each engaged in the effort to extend their respective masters’ sway over the tribe of Benjamin.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **The pool of Gibeon.** Ellicott describes it as “a large reservoir or tank … Its ruins still remain, about 120 feet long by 100 broad.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Joab’s background.** Ellicott identifies Joab as David’s nephew (son of Zeruiah, David’s sister, 1 Chron. 2:16). He was probably among “the brethren of David” at Adullam (1 Sam. 22:1). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Abner sought to make Judah subject “when he had brought all Israel under the dominion of Ishbosheth.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 14: *“Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.”*

- **Single combat to avoid civil war.** Ellicott: “To avoid unnecessary bloodshed between the tribes of a common parentage, and also, perhaps, to prevent the weakening of the nation in the face of their common Philistine foe, Abner proposes that the struggle should be decided by a combat between a few champions.” He compares it to the combat of the Horatii and Curiatii in Livy. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The word translated “compete” (שָׂחַק, śāḥaq) means “to joke or play” — “used here to denote the war-play of single combat.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 15–16: *“Twelve for Benjamin… twelve for David… each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side… they all fell together.”*

- **Mutual slaughter.** Keil & Delitzsch: “One seized the other’s head, and his sword was (immediately) in the side of the other … so that they fell together.” This simultaneous killing demonstrated great ferocity and courage. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik):** “This was diabolical play, where each man thrust his sword into the body of the other, so that the twenty-four (twelve on each side) fell down dead together!” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Helkath-hazzurim.** Most modern expositors (per Ellicott) understand it as “the field of sharp edges” (from ṣūr, “sharp edge”). The older margin reading was “field of strong men,” but “the etymology is very doubtful.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 17: *“The battle that day was intense, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David.”*

- **Decisive but small-scale.** Ellicott: the combat of the twelve having decided nothing, “the two hosts joined battle. Abner and the Israelites were worsted. The numbers engaged were probably not large, as the whole number of the slain was nineteen on David’s side, and 360 on that of Israel.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** “There followed a general and very sore or fierce battle, in which Abner and his troops were put to flight.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 18–19: *“The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel… Asahel was fleet of foot like a wild gazelle, and he chased Abner…”*

- **Asahel’s single-minded pursuit.** Keil & Delitzsch: Asahel “pursued Abner most eagerly, without turning aside to the right or to the left.” He wanted to kill the commander of the opposing army, knowing the enemy cause depended on Abner. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott:** “His great fleetness enabled him to overtake Abner and, coming behind him, endanger his life.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 20–22: *“Abner glanced back… ‘Turn to your right or to your left… Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?’”*

- **Abner’s reluctance — military honor and self-preservation.** Guzik: Abner appealed to Asahel on grounds of military honor — “that officers should not strike down officers, especially when it might lead to ugly retribution.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Abner urged Asahel to “slay one of the common soldiers, and take his accoutrements as booty, if thou art seeking for that kind of fame.” Abner “did not want to put the young hero to death, out of regard for Joab and their former friendship.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott:** Abner’s reluctance was “partly on account of his extreme youth, but was chiefly through dread of the vengeance of Joab.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 23: *“Abner thrust the butt of his spear into his stomach, and it came out his back, and he fell dead on the spot.”*

- **The butt (hinder end) of the spear.** Keil & Delitzsch and Ellicott both explain that the lower end of the spear was pointed so it could be stuck into the ground (cf. 1 Sam. 26:7), which explains how it passed entirely through the body. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott:** “The fifth rib” (KJV) here and elsewhere (2 Sam. 3:27; 4:6; 20:10) “should be translated *abdomen*.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Public mourning.** Keil & Delitzsch: “The fate of the young hero excited such sympathy, that all who came to the place where he had fallen stood still to mourn his loss.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 24–25: *“But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner… The Benjamites rallied to Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand atop a hill.”*

- **Vengeance drives the pursuit.** Guzik: “Now more than the cause of David motivated them. They wanted to avenge the killing of their brother Asahel.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Ellicott:** The rest of Abner’s force was “hopelessly scattered,” but he managed to rally the Benjamites — his and Saul’s kinsmen — “in a strong position on the top of an hill.” Neither Ammah nor Giah can be identified today, but they were likely not far from Gibeon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 26–28: *“Abner called out to Joab: ‘Must the sword devour forever?…’”*

- **Abner’s plea for peace — to his own advantage.** Guzik observes: “When his armies were in full retreat and ready for a final do-or-die stand — and when two angry brothers wanted blood revenge — Abner found it easy to make the plea for peace. It was certainly to his advantage to give peace a chance.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

- **Joab’s reply (“if you had not spoken up…”).** Two interpretations exist (Ellicott): (1) Joab blames Abner — if Abner had not proposed the champion combat, both sides would have separated peaceably at Gibeon. (2) Joab intended to pursue only until morning, but since Abner sued for mercy, he would stop now. Ellicott favors the first. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** “Thus Joab threw all the blame of the fight upon Abner, because he had been the instigator of the single combat; and as that was not decisive, and was so bloody in its character, the two armies had felt obliged to fight it out.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Gray’s Concise Commentary (cited at StudyLight):** “Evidently if Abner had not asked for a stay, Joab would have put it into execution the next day, and for the same reason.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 29: *“All that night Abner and his men marched through the Arabah… crossed the Jordan… and arrived at Mahanaim.”*

- **The Arabah.** Ellicott explains this refers to the Jordan Valley. Abner’s flight had carried him east toward the Jordan; he passed up the valley, crossed at a ford, then went “through all Bithron” (a district east of the Jordan, otherwise unknown) back to Mahanaim. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** “Bithron … is not the name of a city, but of a district … The meaning of the word is ‘a cutting’; it was no doubt the name given to some ravine in the neighbourhood of the Jabbok.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

### vv. 30–31: *“When Joab returned… In addition to Asahel, nineteen of David’s servants were missing, but they had struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner.”*

- **Striking disproportion.** Keil & Delitzsch explain the 360 vs. 20 casualty ratio: “In Joab’s army there were none but brave and well-tried men, who had gathered round David a long time before; whereas in Abner’s army there were only the remnants of the Israelites who had been beaten upon Gilboa.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

- **Ellicott:** The disparity results from “the advantage given by bow and spear … to the pursuer over the pursued,” plus Joab’s men being “long trained under David in hardship and deeds of valour.” It is uncertain whether the twelve champion combatants on each side are included in these numbers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Gray’s Concise Commentary:** “The great value of Asahel is graphically expressed in the words ‘nineteen men *and* Asahel’ (2 Samuel 2:30). He was more than merely a twentieth.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/2-samuel-2.html

### v. 32: *“Later, they took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.”*

- **Burial in Bethlehem.** Ellicott: Ordinary soldiers were buried on the spot; Asahel received special burial “in the sepulchre of his father” because of his position and relationship to David. This reveals that Zeruiah’s husband (otherwise unmentioned) was also of Bethlehem. The burial likely occurred the next day after the battle; the night march to Hebron (about 13 miles) was “chosen … to avoid the heat.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** “It got light to them (i.e., the day dawned) at Hebron.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### David’s Anointing(s) and the Holy Spirit

The **Pentecostal/Charismatic** reading (Enduring Word / David Guzik) emphasizes that the anointing at Hebron was a “fresh anointing” needed after David’s spiritual decline in Ziklag: “This anointing couldn’t come when David still lived among the Philistines virtually as a Philistine.” This frames the anointing in terms of ongoing experience of the Holy Spirit. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

The **Reformed/older conservative** reading (Keil & Delitzsch) treats the three anointings more as progressive public recognition of a divine decree already given, with no particular emphasis on a “fresh” experience. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

The **Evangelical/Baptist** (Precept Austin, citing multiple teachers) focuses on David’s patient waiting and submission to God’s timing, using the passage devotionally: “We may know the LORD’s will … but from David, we learn that waiting may be what the LORD is calling us to do.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-2-commentary

### The Cease-Fire at Gibeon — Wisdom or Folly?

Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic) argues the cease-fire was actually a mistake: “This shows how wrong it was for Joab to accept Abner’s appeal … The cease-fire seemed to make things better, but in reality, it only made things worse and it led to a long war.” He applies this spiritually: “When we try to make peace between King Jesus and king self within us, the result is a long, bitter war.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/

The **older commentaries** (Gray’s Concise, Ellicott) treat the cease-fire more neutrally as a pragmatic military decision — Abner asked for it to save his routed army; Joab granted it to rest his exhausted forces. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/2-samuel-2.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-2.html

### Ish-bosheth as a “Puppet King”

The **Keil & Delitzsch** commentary goes furthest in condemning Abner’s action as “an open act of rebellion against Jehovah.” For them, the theological dimension is primary: God had clearly chosen David, and Abner acted against the revealed will of God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-samuel-2.html

Guzik reads the same event more pragmatically: Abner set up a weak king to be the real power behind the throne, and David’s patience in not crushing him “showed remarkable patience, longsuffering, and trust in God.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-2/
